name: Caro-Kann Defense
description: The Caro-Kann is a solid defense for Black against 1.e4. You play 1...c6 preparing to push d5, which challenges White's center without blocking your light-squared bishop. It's an excellent choice for beginners who want safe, principled play.
whyPlayIt: The Caro-Kann gives Black a solid pawn structure and active piece play without needing to memorize deep theory. Unlike the French Defense, your light-squared bishop stays free — one of Black's biggest advantages.
keyIdeas: Play c6 first to prepare d5 — this challenges White's center while keeping the light-squared bishop unblocked.
After dxe4, develop the bishop to f5 BEFORE playing e6, which would lock it in — this is the defining advantage over the French Defense.
Aim for a solid, slightly passive but unbreakable position, then gradually improve your pieces while White struggles to break through.

mainLine.explanation: White plays e4, the most popular first move. Now we respond with the Caro-Kann: 1...c6.
The Caro-Kann move! We prepare d5 to challenge White's center. Unlike the French Defense (1...e6), this doesn't block our light-squared bishop.
White builds a strong pawn center with d4. This is the most ambitious response.
Now we challenge the center with d5! This is what c6 was preparing. We have a solid pawn on d5 backed by c6.
White defends e4 with the knight. This leads to the Classical Caro-Kann — one of the sharpest lines.
We capture on e4! This exchange releases the tension and starts the Classical variation. Now White must recapture.
White recaptures with the knight, centralizing it powerfully. Now we play 4...Bf5, the most important move!
Bf5 is the key move! We develop our light-squared bishop BEFORE playing e6, which would lock it in. This is the big advantage of the Caro-Kann over the French.
White attacks our bishop with Ng3. Don't retreat to e6 — that blocks your pawn! Play Bg6 instead.
Bg6 retreats the bishop to a safe square where it still has long-term influence. We have a very solid position! Classical Caro-Kann line complete.

variations.name: Advance Variation

moves.explanation: White plays e5, the Advance Variation — grabbing more space. Don't panic! We have a clear plan: develop the bishop outside the chain with Bf5.
Bf5! Get the bishop out before playing e6. This is the same idea as the Classical — develop your bishops before closing the pawn chain.
White develops the knight. Now we play e6, closing the pawn chain — but our bishop is already safely developed!
e6 solidifies our pawn structure. The bishop is already on f5, safe and active — unlike the French where it gets locked in.
White develops the bishop. Now we play Nd7, preparing to challenge the e5 pawn.
Nd7 develops a piece and prepares ...Ne7 to challenge the e5 pawn later. We have a very solid setup. Advance Variation line complete!

variations.explanation: The Advance Variation (3.e5) gives White more space but we get easy piece play with Bf5 and e6.

variations.name: Exchange Variation

moves.explanation: White plays exd5, the Exchange Variation — trading pawns to simplify. We recapture with cxd5.
cxd5 recaptures, giving us a strong central pawn on d5. The Exchange Variation leads to very equal positions — good for beginners who want simplicity.
White develops the bishop to d3, eyeing our kingside. We develop our pieces naturally.
Nc6 develops with tempo, putting pressure on d4. We're building a solid position with active pieces.
White supports d4 with c3. Now we play Nf6, completing development.
Nf6 develops the knight to its ideal square. We have two active knights and a solid pawn on d5. Exchange Variation line complete!

variations.explanation: The Exchange Variation creates symmetrical, simplified positions — a good choice if you want quiet, technical play.

commonAmateurResponses.name: 2.Bc4 before building center
commonAmateurResponses.description: Some beginners play 2.Bc4 immediately, hoping to attack f7, but this doesn't work against the Caro-Kann setup.

moves.explanation: White plays e4.
We play c6.
White tries Bc4, eyeing f7.

commonAmateurResponses.refutation: Play d5 immediately — e.g. 2...d5 3.exd5 cxd5 and the bishop on c4 is misplaced. You get a great version of the Caro-Kann Exchange.

commonAmateurResponses.name: 2.Nc3 without d4
commonAmateurResponses.description: Playing Nc3 without first securing d4 gives Black an easy game.

moves.explanation: White plays e4.
We play c6.
White develops the knight without d4.

commonAmateurResponses.refutation: Simply play d5 and achieve a perfectly comfortable position. Without d4 established, White can't control the center firmly.

trapsToKnow.name: The Bf5 Before e6 Principle
trapsToKnow.description: In the Classical Caro-Kann, beginners often forget to play Bf5 before e6, accidentally locking in their bishop.

moves.explanation: White recaptures with the knight. This is the critical moment.
Bf5 NOW, before e6! This is the entire point of the Caro-Kann.

trapsToKnow.lesson: Always remember: in the Classical Caro-Kann, you MUST play Bf5 before e6 or you get a French Defense with an extra tempo for White — which is much worse!
